items.title: Binance Lost $6.3 Billion. Who Signed the Withdrawals?
items.summary: Most of the money moved in about twenty minutes. The blockchain recorded valid instructions. The harder question was who had the power to give them.
items.content_html:
At 20:05 UTC on Thursday, October 29, funds began leaving Binance hot wallets. An XRP holder could have spent the evening with their phone off, their password secret and their two-factor key in a drawer. None of those precautions would have stopped a transfer from a wallet the exchange operated. The customer’s phone was never in that signing path.

Two accounts of the breach matter. Binance can investigate what happened inside its systems. Outside investigators can reconstruct what those systems told blockchains to do. Where the two accounts meet, we learn something practical about keeping money on a phone.

What the chain can tell us

TRM Labs traced roughly $6.36 billion across ten blockchains. On Ethereum, it found a signed authorization that let one of Binance’s hot wallets run code chosen by the attacker. That code could sweep assets out. Think of the difference between signing one cheque and authorizing someone to write subsequent cheques. On the other nine chains TRM examined, the money moved through ordinary signed transfers. The Ethereum mechanism explains one part of the theft. It cannot explain all ten chains. TRM’s on-chain reconstruction

Who obtained the authority to sign? Binance initially pointed to a possibly compromised engineer’s laptop and access to a service container that could submit withdrawals. Its next bulletin said investigators had found additional points of entry. At that stage the company had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys. That wording matters. A thief who can persuade a legitimate signer to act may never need a copy of its key. A valid signature alone cannot tell us which computer the attacker first entered. Binance’s initial account · Its follow-up

Three figures in the headlines described different things. Binance put the theft at about $6.3 billion. It reported that partners had frozen about $3 billion on-chain. On October 31 it said it had replenished 90% of affected assets, drawing on reserves and company resources. Freezing can stop a thief spending an asset. Replenishing can make customers whole using different assets. Adding those figures would count different stages of the same response. On November 1 Binance announced a phased reopening of withdrawals. Replenishment update · Withdrawal update

Four cases from the past twelve months

The chart compares four documented exchange incidents between November 1, 2025 and October 31, 2026. Each dot marks the approximate value moved at the time, before recovery or reimbursement. Equal distances on the scale represent tenfold increases. These cases illustrate different failures. They are a selection, so they cannot tell us how often exchanges are breached.

Upbit, November 27, 2025. Solana-based assets worth about ₩44.5 billion, roughly $30 million at the time, went to an unauthorized external address. Upbit’s emergency review identified a wallet weakness that it patched. Finding a weakness during an investigation does not demonstrate the thieves used it. For this case, the transfer and amount are better established than the route in. Upbit’s notice · Contemporaneous reporting

Bitget, September 24, 2026. Here the operator gave a much more specific account. An attacker exploited a flaw in a third-party security product, obtained powerful internal credentials, then issued fraudulent withdrawal commands. Twelve hot or warm wallet addresses were affected. Bitget ultimately put the value at about $388 million. Its timeline records 34 minutes between the first abnormal transfer and the reconciliation alarm that blocked withdrawals. Customer login security could do little about an instruction that already looked internal. Bitget’s investigation and timeline

CoinDCX, October 21, 2026, disclosed in detail October 25. An old deposit address kept receiving money after the exchange retired it. CoinDCX continued crediting customers and ran a service to sweep those funds into current wallets. When the sweeper stopped working for a period, deposits accumulated at an address on previously compromised infrastructure. CoinDCX says it absorbed a loss of 15.99 million USDT. A retired address can disappear from an app while remaining perfectly capable of receiving money on-chain. CoinDCX’s account

Binance, October 29, 2026. The fourth dot is so far from the others that it helps to put it in words. Binance’s initial $6.3 billion estimate was about sixteen times Bitget’s $388 million. The size tells us how much one signing environment could reach. It tells us very little about an individual customer’s password habits.

Move the signer, and the risk moves with it

Open an exchange app and tap Withdraw. You ask a company to move funds. It can inspect your request, pause it during an incident, replace missing assets from its treasury, or deny the withdrawal. Open a personal software wallet and tap Send. The usual path is shorter. Your device prepares and signs a transaction, then a network provider broadcasts it. There is no exchange withdrawal desk in that path.

We publish Oath Wallet, so you should be able to check our side of that comparison. The public iPhone and iPad wallet stores recovery material in an encrypted local vault and signs on the device. The application source for version 4.1.15, build 100, is public under the MIT license. Take one concrete path through it. Before signing an ordinary Ethereum-family send, the code checks that the account belongs to the wallet, the network matches the plan, and the sender is the expected address. The network receives a signed transaction. It does not need the recovery phrase to relay it. Read the release source · Inspect the signing function

For someone holding their own keys, that changes two things at once. Oath has no company withdrawal key for that personal wallet. Oath support also cannot replace a lost recovery secret. A deliberate export or an optional encrypted iCloud backup creates another copy to protect. An imported phrase carries its history with it. If somebody copied it before you installed Oath, installing a new wallet does not revoke their copy. The public review records tested fixes and remaining gaps so readers can judge the evidence themselves. Public build and backup behavior · Review evidence

The signature that never asks for your words

Suppose a site offers to check whether you qualify for a refund. It opens your wallet. The screen shows a token approval with a spender address and a very large limit. If you approve it, that spender may later transfer those tokens within the allowance. Your recovery phrase can stay on paper in a locked drawer the entire time. This familiar token allowance is a different permission from the account delegation seen in the Binance case, but it makes the same point in everyday terms. The words you keep secret and the instructions you sign protect different things. How ERC-20 allowances work

If you encounter that screen, read the verb first. Sending pays a recipient. Approving gives a spender an allowance. Delegating can give code authority over an account. Then read the network, asset, address and amount. If you came to check a balance and the request grants spending rights, close it. If you already granted a token allowance, disconnecting a site does not revoke the on-chain permission.

There is a quieter test of custody than any promise on a wallet’s home page. Imagine the company’s withdrawal service goes offline tonight. Could you still use your recovery material in compatible software to send your funds tomorrow? Then ask the reverse question. If your phone and every usable backup disappeared tonight, who could restore access for you? Those two answers tell you where your money’s real dependencies live.

items.title: The Missing Link Between Open Source and the Wallet on Your Phone
items.summary: What connects public source code to the app you install? A practical guide to reproducible builds, signed releases, App Store approval, and Oath’s current evidence.
items.content_html:
You find a wallet with a public GitHub repository. The code is there. The license is there. People can inspect it, discuss it, and build it themselves. That is a meaningful reason to pay attention.

Then you open the App Store and tap Download.

One question still needs an answer: was the app you just installed actually built from the code you were shown?

For a wallet, that question reaches all the way to your money. The software on your phone helps generate or import credentials, displays the transaction you are about to authorize, and signs it. Being able to inspect the source is valuable. Being able to connect that source to the distributed app adds another layer of assurance.

Here is what that extra layer means, what it can prove, and how Oath describes the relationship between its public source and its App Store release.

What open source gives you

Open-source software makes its code available under a license that grants rights to use, study, modify, and redistribute it. The Open Source Initiative’s definition includes those freedoms; simply putting some code on a public page does not automatically meet the definition. Read the Open Source Definition.

For a wallet, public source lets independent developers examine questions that a marketing page cannot settle. How are keys generated? What gets stored? What leaves the device? What must happen before a transaction is signed? Which third-party libraries are involved?

That scrutiny matters even if you never read a line of code yourself. Researchers and other developers can investigate on your behalf and publish findings that everyone can inspect.

But a repository describes a body of code. On its own, it does not establish which code produced a particular download. A developer could publish one version and distribute another. A build system could also introduce an unwanted change after a reviewer has examined the source. Those are the gaps that build verification aims to reduce. The Reproducible Builds project explains this threat.

What a reproducible build adds

A build turns source code into the software your device runs. A reproducible build makes that transformation repeatable: with the specified source, environment, and instructions, another party can produce identical copies of the defined output files. The comparison is usually made using cryptographic hashes. See the formal definition.

A meaningful verification result therefore connects three things: an exact source revision, a documented build process, and a precisely identified release artifact. The report should show what was compared and whether it matched.

There is an extra step when the claim concerns an app store. Matching an unsigned file hosted on GitHub establishes a result about that file. To establish a result about the app on your phone, the evidence must also connect the comparison to the artifact delivered through that store.

Consider two otherwise comparable wallets. Both publish their source. For one, the connection between source and download rests on the publisher’s assurance. For the other, an independent party can rebuild the stated release and verify the distributed artifact using a documented method. The second offers stronger evidence against an undisclosed difference introduced during building or distribution. That is the specific security advantage.

The word “verified” needs an object

Several useful checks are often described with the same word. They answer different questions.

A verified GitHub commit means GitHub has verified a commit’s cryptographic signature. It says something about the origin and integrity of that commit. It does not compare an App Store download with the repository. GitHub documents exactly what its badge means.

A successful build or test run establishes that the stated build or tests completed in that environment. It does not establish that a store serves the same output.

A signed release provides evidence about the signer and the integrity of the signed artifact. A developer’s signature does not, by itself, demonstrate that the artifact was produced from public source.

A build attestation records provenance: information such as the source commit, repository, and workflow associated with an artifact. This is valuable evidence, but it still needs verification against the artifact and a sensible trust policy. GitHub explicitly warns that attestations do not guarantee an artifact is secure. Read GitHub’s explanation of artifact attestations.

An independently reproduced release adds a rebuild-and-compare result. A claim about the store version must identify how that result reaches the store-delivered app.

Before accepting “verified build,” ask: verified by whom, against what, and for which version?

Apple’s approval and the source-to-store question

Apple’s review and code-signing system provide real protections. Apple describes developer identity checks, mandatory code signing, and review intended to check that apps generally work as described. These establish a controlled distribution process. They do not constitute a published comparison with a wallet’s GitHub source. Apple explains its app code-signing process.

The artifact itself also needs careful treatment. Apple’s app-thinning documentation describes device-specific variants containing different combinations of assets and binaries. A universal archive and a device-specific download can therefore be different files for legitimate reasons. See Apple’s documentation on app variants.

A credible iOS verification method must identify the exact version and build, the source revision, the toolchain and configuration, and the particular artifact or components compared. It must explain how platform packaging and signing are handled. If any parts are excluded from comparison, the report needs to say which parts and why.

A matching version number, an archive checksum, or a successful upload is useful release bookkeeping. None of those facts alone closes the source-to-store gap.

When a wallet says its App Store build is verified, you should be able to follow a method and inspect a result, rather than infer a result from Apple’s approval.

Google Play needs a precise claim, too

Android has practical tools for reproducible verification, but the distribution route still matters. Google Play can generate and sign optimized APKs from an Android App Bundle for different device configurations. Verifying an APK from a project’s website does not automatically verify every Play-delivered variant. Google explains how App Bundles are distributed.

F-Droid documents a concrete approach: reproduce the upstream APK, copy its signing information using the supported method, and check that verification succeeds. Its documentation explains both the required equivalence and common causes of mismatches. That is the kind of inspectable process a reproducibility claim should point to. Read F-Droid’s reproducible-build documentation.

How to compare wallets fairly

There are useful examples worth recognizing. Muun’s Android repository includes instructions for reproducible builds and for checking an existing APK: obtain the installed APK, select the corresponding source commit, and run its verification script. That goes beyond a general statement that the source is public. This article reviews the published procedure; it does not report a fresh verification of Muun’s current release, and the Android procedure should not be treated as proof for iOS. Muun’s Android build and verification instructions.

Blockstream’s Android README documents another useful check: verifying release authenticity through certificate fingerprints and signed checksums. Those instructions help authenticate the download. The check described there answers a different question from independently rebuilding it. This is a distinction between the methods, not a claim that those instructions describe all of Blockstream’s security work. Blockstream’s release-authenticity instructions.

For any wallet that offers only a repository link, the fair conclusion is limited: public source is available, but that link alone supplies no evidence of a store-binary match. It would be wrong to turn that absence into an accusation of malicious behavior. It would also be wrong to advertise a match without evidence.

Compare the platform, release, method, and result. A brand-wide label hides too much.

Oath: open source, and a clear statement about the shipped app

Oath publishes its MIT-licensed 4.1.14 (98) source release with build instructions and a release verification record. The app source used for the uploaded archive is commit v4.1.14. Provider configuration and Apple signing are supplied locally and excluded from Git. Explore Oath’s published source release.

On October 30, 2026, build 86 was uploaded to App Store Connect and submitted for review. The release verification record records the source, archive and upload evidence. Apple showed Waiting for Review at submission; the public US App Store listing still showed 4.1.2 when checked. Submission is not approval or a new public-store binary comparison.

There is a distinction worth keeping explicit: a publisher’s confirmation is not the same evidence as an independent party reproducing a release and publishing its comparison. This article does not present a new binary comparison, a byte-for-byte reproducibility result, or an independent security audit. The repository’s documented exclusions and configuration requirements still apply.

That distinction is the point of this article. Public source gives people something concrete to inspect. A maintainer’s release statement makes the team’s claim explicit. An independently repeatable comparison provides a further level of evidence. Readers should be able to tell which of those they are looking at.

For Oath, as for every wallet, security language should help people understand the evidence. It should never make them guess what “verified” means.

Five things to look for before trusting a build claim

  1. An exact release. The platform, version, build number, and distribution channel should be unambiguous.
  2. An exact source revision. A fixed commit is more useful than a moving default branch.
  3. A repeatable recipe. Toolchain versions, dependencies, configuration, and required build inputs should be documented.
  4. A transparent comparison. Look for artifact identifiers, the comparison method, the result, and any exclusions.
  5. A named verifier and a date. Distinguish a publisher’s own checks from independent reproduction, and check whether the result applies to the version you use.

The Reproducible Builds guidance on build environments explains why the toolchain and its assumptions need to be documented.

You should never need to share a recovery phrase or private key to investigate a public build-verification claim.

Better evidence, with honest limits

A reproducible build can faithfully reproduce vulnerable code. It cannot, by itself, establish that the design is sound, that a remote service is trustworthy, or that your phone is uncompromised. Source review, security testing, careful dependency management, and responsible release practices still matter. Reproducibility addresses a particular gap in that larger system. Read more about its purpose and limits.

Open source makes inspection possible. Reproducible builds make a specified source-to-artifact relationship testable. Verification of the distributed app brings that evidence closer to the software you actually use.

For self-custody, those distinctions deserve plain language. A wallet should make it easy to see what has been checked, what the result proves, and what remains unproven. Confidence is more useful when you can trace where it comes from.

Published October 19, 2026. Oath release evidence updated October 30, 2026. Oath’s source-correspondence statement is supplied by its maintainers. The technical explanations cite public documentation; this article is not an independent wallet audit or a new reproduction of an App Store or Google Play release.

items.title: Your Crypto, Their Permission: The $388 Million Bitget Wake-Up Call
items.summary: Bitget’s $388 million breach exposes the difference between a protected balance and control of your money. A sourced examination of exchange failures, self-custody, and the responsibilities that come with your keys.
items.content_html:
An exchange can promise to replace stolen money. It cannot give you back the moment you needed to move it.

That distinction is easy to overlook when markets are calm. Your balance appears on a screen. You can buy, sell, and watch its value change. The experience feels like possession. Only when withdrawals stop does the underlying arrangement become visible: someone else has the authority to release your assets.

Bitget’s September 24 security breach has made that arrangement painfully concrete. The exchange initially estimated the loss at $351.6 million, then revised it to $387.5 million after identifying additional affected transfers. Its latest public account rounds the figure to approximately $388 million. These are estimates of assets taken from exchange infrastructure—not evidence that customers individually suffered equivalent, unreimbursed losses. Bitget’s September 25 update; updated incident account.

The distinction matters. So does the fact that customers could not withdraw while the exchange repaired its systems.

We build Oath Wallet because we believe people should be able to hold and use their crypto without relying on an exchange’s permission. But the case for self-custody deserves more than a slogan, and readers deserve more than a frightening headline. It requires a careful account of what failed, what an exchange can actually promise, and which responsibilities move to you when you take control of your keys.

What actually happened at Bitget

The incident affected Bitget’s centralized exchange. Bitget Wallet, its separate non-custodial product, was not affected, according to Bitget. Confusing those products would obscure the very distinction this story illustrates. Bitget’s incident account.

The exchange’s September 25 update reported unauthorized transfers across several networks, including assets on Ethereum and other EVM chains, XRP Ledger, Zcash, and TRON. The upward revision from $351.6 million to $387.5 million reflected a fuller accounting, including Zcash and TRON transfers omitted initially. Bitget said the revision did not indicate a second attack or further transfers after containment. It also announced recovery bounties for qualifying assistance in freezing or recovering funds. Official fund-tracing and recovery update.

The attackers did not necessarily need to steal the keys

Bitget’s current explanation is preliminary: an attacker may have exploited a third-party security product to obtain privileged internal credentials, then used them to issue fraudulent withdrawal commands. The exchange says private-key compromise has been ruled out in its investigation to date, and its cold wallets were unaffected. Mandiant and SlowMist are supporting the continuing investigation. Bitget’s incident account.

Blockchain investigator TRM Labs described the reported failure as manipulation of the information used to authorize transfers. Its analysis also traced the dispersal of stolen funds and routes through cross-chain services. TRM identified links suggesting North Korean involvement but stopped short of definitive attribution. That uncertainty belongs in any responsible account of the breach. TRM Labs’ analysis.

The security lesson is broader than the identity of the attacker. A private key can remain secret while the machinery surrounding it authorizes a disastrous transaction. A signing system answers a cryptographic question: was this transaction approved by the required key? It does not, by itself, establish that the human intention behind the transaction was honest or correctly understood.

For an exchange customer, this creates a difficult boundary. You can secure your password, protect your email, and use strong authentication. You cannot personally inspect every privileged credential, third-party dependency, withdrawal rule, or internal approval process at the exchange. Your account security and the institution’s custody security are related, but they are different systems.

The pause exposed who controlled access

Bitget’s updated chronology places the first unauthorized transfers at 18:31 UTC on September 24. It says reconciliation detected a discrepancy and automatically blocked withdrawals at 19:05; withdrawal and signing services were shut down at 21:44. These are the company’s reported timings, not our independent forensic reconstruction. Updated incident timeline.

Pausing a compromised withdrawal system can be the responsible response. Continuing to operate it could expose more assets. The problem for customers is that the same measure needed to protect the collective pool also prevents an individual from leaving it.

That is a structural limitation of custodial protection. A platform can have a good reason to suspend withdrawals, yet the customer still loses the ability to act. There need be no dishonesty, insolvency, or malicious intent for this loss of control to occur.

The recovery is part of the story, too

Bitget says customer balances remain unaffected and its Protection Fund covers the incident’s financial impact. Its published schedule proposed reopening BTC withdrawals on September 28, ETH on September 29, USDT on September 30, and remaining supported tokens, fiat withdrawals, and P2P services on October 2, each at 08:00 UTC. Those later dates remain a schedule, not completed milestones as of this article. Bitget’s withdrawal announcement.

On September 28, The Block reported that Bitget had begun processing Bitcoin withdrawals as scheduled. That is meaningful progress and should be acknowledged plainly. This is an account of a breach and a staged restoration of access—not a claim that Bitget has collapsed or that all customer money is gone. The Block’s September 28 report.

Nevertheless, restoring access after an interruption is different from having maintained it. Consider a person who needs to pay a supplier, meet an obligation, or move funds into a safer arrangement. Even if their eventual balance is preserved, their choices during the interruption were constrained. This is an illustration of the risk, not a claim about a particular Bitget customer.

A complete definition of protection must include access as well as reimbursement.

A protection fund is useful. It does not confer control.

A sufficiently funded reserve can prevent a platform theft from becoming a customer loss. Customers should welcome that protection. TRM’s September 25 account cited a Bitget protection fund of approximately $464 million and the exchange’s statement that it covered the loss. That is a reported figure from that date, not a claim about the fund’s balance today. TRM Labs.

But a reserve changes who may absorb a financial loss; it does not change who authorizes withdrawals. The customer still depends on the institution to assess the incident, deploy resources, repair infrastructure, and restore service.

When evaluating any protection fund, useful questions concern its assets, custody, scope, exclusions, legal commitments, and ability to cover multiple events. A headline dollar amount cannot answer those questions on its own. Nor should a privately maintained fund be casually described as equivalent to government deposit insurance.

The same discipline applies to proof of reserves. The PCAOB’s Office of the Investor Advocate has warned that these reports are not audits and may omit liabilities, asset-holder rights, borrowed reserves, and the effectiveness of governance or internal controls. They are also tied to a point in time. PCAOB investor advisory.

An exchange can hold substantial assets and still suffer a failure in the process that moves them. Financial resilience and operational security answer different questions. Neither gives a depositor a personal signing key for the exchange’s pooled funds.

Three earlier failures, three different warnings

It would be misleading to treat every exchange crisis as the same event. Theft, fraud, and prolonged insolvency proceedings have different causes and different outcomes. They nevertheless expose a recurring dependency: customers must wait for decisions made elsewhere.

Mt. Gox: the cost measured in years

Mt. Gox’s trustee was already reporting on bankruptcy proceedings and the recovery of assets in July 2014. A decade later, in June 2024, the rehabilitation trustee announced that Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash repayments would begin that July. The notice described the technical, regulatory, and coordination work required before repayment. 2014 trustee report; 2024 repayment notice.

The lesson is not captured by a missing-coin total alone. It is the interval between believing an asset is available and having the freedom to use what can eventually be recovered.

During such an interval, an owner’s life continues. Expenses arrive; circumstances change. A claim handled through a rehabilitation process is not operationally equivalent to bitcoin that the holder can transfer. Eventual distributions matter, but they do not erase the years in between.

FTX: account security could not stop insider misuse

FTX illustrates a different failure. In March 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Sam Bankman-Fried’s 25-year prison sentence. It described the misappropriation of billions of dollars deposited by customers, including their use for investments, political contributions, and repayment of Alameda Research’s debts. Prosecutors put the theft of customer money at more than $8 billion. U.S. Department of Justice.

No customer could fix that arrangement by choosing a stronger login password. The central problem was what people inside the institution could do with assets entrusted to them.

This does not establish that other exchanges behave like FTX. It establishes why custody requires scrutiny of governance, segregation, legal rights, and business incentives—not merely the appearance of a polished application. A clean interface tells you little about authority behind it.

Bybit: cold storage still depended on a signing workflow

The FBI attributed the theft of approximately $1.5 billion from Bybit on or about February 21, 2025, to North Korea. Bybit subsequently reported that compromised credentials belonging to a Safe developer enabled an attack that deceived signers into approving a malicious transaction. FBI public notice; Bybit’s February 26 investigation update.

Cold storage reduces exposure, but assets eventually have to move. The process that interprets and authorizes that movement remains part of the security system. This is relevant to institutions and individual users alike: multiple signatures and protected keys are valuable, but they cannot make an inaccurately understood transaction safe.

Mt. Gox, FTX, Bybit, and Bitget should not be collapsed into one accusation. Their shared lesson is narrower and stronger: control of assets depends on the entire custody arrangement, including the people, software, and procedures permitted to move them.

What self-custody changes

A wallet does not literally contain coins. It manages the keys and related information needed to interact with assets recorded on a blockchain. With genuine self-custody, you control the credentials that authorize spending instead of asking an exchange to authorize a withdrawal. The SEC’s custody bulletin explains this distinction and the responsibilities it creates. Investor.gov: crypto asset custody basics.

That change has several practical consequences.

An exchange’s withdrawal policy stops governing those assets. Once assets have been transferred to a wallet you control, a trading platform cannot impose its own withdrawal queue on that wallet. Your ability to transact still depends on the network, fees, valid credentials, and the rules of the asset itself.

The exchange’s balance sheet stops being the custody foundation for those holdings. If you keep native assets under your own keys, you do not need that exchange to remain solvent to authorize a transaction. This advantage disappears for funds you subsequently deposit into a custodial service. It also should not be confused with eliminating the separate risks of stablecoin issuers, bridges, or lending protocols.

You can choose how much authority to expose. Daily spending, long-term holdings, and experimental applications do not have to share one wallet. Separating them can limit the consequences of a mistake. Merely adding more accounts derived from the same exposed recovery phrase does not provide that isolation.

Recovery can be designed around credentials you control. For a standard recovery-phrase wallet, retaining the correct phrase—and any additional passphrase and necessary account information—can allow restoration in compatible software. Compatibility and the precise backup requirements must be checked before they are needed.

These are concrete reasons self-custody can be a better arrangement for long-term holders who are prepared to manage it. It removes the exchange’s discretionary control over the assets held that way. It does not make every transaction, token, device, or wallet safe.

The responsibilities that come with the keys

A serious defense of self-custody must address its failures as carefully as those of exchanges.

If your recovery material is stolen, an attacker may gain the same spending authority you have. If the only usable recovery material is lost, there may be no institution able to restore access. The SEC’s custody guidance emphasizes that self-custody places responsibility for private-key security on the holder. Investor.gov custody bulletin.

And a key need not be stolen for a user to approve something harmful. In December 2023, the Ledger Connect Kit incident injected malicious code into applications using the affected library and tricked users into signing asset-draining transactions, according to Ledger’s incident report. That was an attack on a connection and signing experience, not evidence that every Ledger hardware device had been broken. Ledger’s security incident report.

The point is uncomfortable but necessary: a self-custody wallet can faithfully execute the wrong instruction. A convincing screen, urgent message, or apparently familiar website can induce that instruction.

Self-custody also leaves other risks intact. Asset prices can fall. Networks can become congested. Smart contracts can contain vulnerabilities. Some tokens give issuers administrative powers; holding their keys does not remove those powers. Hardware can fail, software can contain defects, and backups can be incomplete.

For someone unable to maintain safe recovery procedures, a well-chosen custody service may be preferable to an improvised setup they do not understand. The right response is to develop competence gradually. Moving everything at once out of fear can replace one serious risk with another.

The relevant question is which risks you can understand, reduce, and bear—not which product promises a life without risk.

A practical way to take control

Moving toward self-custody is a process of verification. It should feel deliberate.

  1. Separate trading from holding. Decide what actually needs to remain on an exchange for near-term activity. A convenient trading account does not have to become the permanent home of every asset you own.
  2. Create the wallet through a verified source. Use the provider’s authentic distribution channel. Never adopt a recovery phrase supplied by a stranger, a supposed support agent, or a website offering a pre-funded wallet.
  3. Understand the backup before adding meaningful funds. Know exactly what restores access, how it is protected, and what happens if your phone is lost. Check the wallet’s supported recovery procedure without entering secrets into a website, chat, or untrusted device. Never erase your only working wallet to “test” an uncertain backup.
  4. Check the asset and network on both ends. Similar names and matching-looking addresses are not enough. Confirm that the receiving wallet supports the exact asset on the exact withdrawal network, including any required memo or destination tag.
  5. Make a small test transfer. Verify receipt and the ability to use the funds before moving more. Where appropriate, test a small outgoing transaction too. A successful test establishes that particular route; it does not guarantee future safety.
  6. Keep long-term holdings away from casual signing. Consider hardware-backed arrangements for substantial holdings, and assess whether you can operate them safely. Use separate credentials for experimental activity. Read permissions and transaction details rather than approving by habit.
  7. Plan for loss, incapacity, and inheritance. A recovery method that only works while you are present and remember everything is unfinished. Document a secure process without leaving all the ingredients for theft together.

If an exchange has paused withdrawals, do not trust messages offering a special exit, priority approval, or paid recovery shortcut. Follow verified announcements and wait for the relevant withdrawal route to reopen. No legitimate support conversation requires your wallet’s recovery phrase.

These practices cannot guarantee safety. They can make control informed and usable.

Why we build Oath Wallet

Oath Wallet is built around a simple commitment: the wallet should serve the person who holds it. Our product overview describes that approach, and our source repository is available for inspection.

We believe a wallet should make receiving, holding, sending, and recovery understandable. A user should be able to distinguish a transaction from an approval, a backup from a login, and a wallet balance from a platform’s promise. Good design helps people notice the decisions that matter.

Our preference for self-custody does not give us permission to make absolute claims. Open source creates an opportunity for scrutiny; it is not proof that software has no vulnerabilities. A readable interface helps; it cannot remove the need for careful decisions. No wallet provider, including Oath Wallet, should ask people to abandon judgment in exchange for a reassuring brand.

The point is to place meaningful authority with the user and make the responsibilities of that authority clear.

The question to ask before the next incident

When an exchange suffers a breach, attention naturally turns to the amount stolen, the suspected attacker, and the size of the recovery fund. Those are essential facts. They are not the only facts a customer needs.

Ask a more personal question: if this institution closes its withdrawal system tonight, what can I still do with my assets tomorrow?

If the answer depends entirely on that institution’s timetable, you have identified a custody dependency. Strong authentication, visible reserves, and responsible incident management may reduce parts of the risk. They do not remove that dependency.

Bitget’s recovery efforts deserve fair reporting. Its breach still demonstrates why protection cannot be measured only by whether a company ultimately absorbs a loss. People also need the ability to act.

Self-custody, practiced carefully, gives that ability a different foundation: credentials you control, backups you understand, and transactions you choose to authorize.

A balance is reassuring. The authority to use it is what makes it yours in practice.

Reporting note: researched and updated on September 28, 2026. The Bitget investigation and withdrawal restoration remain in progress. Company statements are identified as such; attribution and preliminary technical explanations should not be treated as final forensic findings. The headline rounds the September 25 estimate of $387.5 million to $388 million, consistent with Bitget’s latest public account. This article is published by Oath Wallet, a self-custody wallet provider, and explains our editorial position rather than offering individualized investment advice.

  • Bitget: updated incident explanation, chronology, product distinction, and investigation status.

items.title: Bitcoin Address Types and Recovery Scope in Oath
items.summary: Match the address type and imported key scope; changing the visible format does not change the blockchain.
items.content_html:
Updated November 2, 2026 · source 5.0.0 (102)

Current release guidance

Checked against the 5.0.0 source. Check the version installed on your phone against the tagged source. Older screenshots are illustrative and may show controls absent from this release.

Available address families

For compatible Bitcoin wallets, Receive offers Taproot (BIP86), Native SegWit (BIP84), nested SegWit (BIP49) and Legacy (BIP44). The available choices depend on your imported material. An uncompressed single key supports Legacy only; a scoped extended key cannot recreate unrelated branches.

Receive and change

A new receiving address can belong to the same wallet. Change addresses account for value returned to your wallet by a transaction. The scan covers supported imported branches rather than only the currently selected display type. It does not guarantee discovery beyond the implemented account and gap rules.

Electrum and aezeed

These are Bitcoin-specific recovery formats. Preserve the original seed extension or password. Aezeed account-zero recovery covers supported on-chain paths; it does not recover Lightning channels or arbitrary custom accounts.

Unsupported recovery methods

Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 5.0.0. Do not treat an sp1 destination as ordinary Taproot, and do not assume an old BRD-specific recovery menu or screenshot exists in this build. Keep the original wallet when the required account format is unsupported.

Before sending or receiving

Confirm the exact network, full recipient address and required fee. Refresh and compare known addresses before relying on a restore. A published example address or screenshot is not a receiving address for your wallet.

See the current security model, Help Center, and release verification record. Never share recovery words, private keys or backup passwords with support.

items.summary: Oath now supports WalletConnect. Understand the difference between a session, a signature and an on-chain approval.
